prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Anything, Desperately, But

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished, eloquent version of the text formatted as sophisticated literary prose. Every detail, imagery, date, scientific reference, and metaphor from the original has been carefully preserved:

***

I desperately require everything else—anything else—yet I possess nothing and shall have nothing save for this: an experience immediate, inescapable, and beyond price. No one can truly afford *this*, which is taking shape here and now in Seattle, Washington, on the 17th of May, 1955.

Marigolds. Concise, almost wooden, and vividly orange. Behind them stands the garage door, painted pink under the fatuous shade name "Old Rose"—a title that inexplicably summons memories of war. 

Unbidden, the mind slides over the fence once more, captured by the uncontrollable juxtaposition of orange against pink and green. It returns of its own accord, offering no explanation and giving no account. Of what use is it? What value does it hold? It is dying! 

You have less than a second to live—less than a second to attempt an explanation. One might argue that light, traveling in specific wavelengths or oscillating bundles at a given velocity, produces the sensory phenomenon of orange against pink. 

Is it superior to a fine sirloin steak? Or a decorative screen by Kōrin? When absorbed internally, the effect of this beauty upon the mind has no equivalent. Least equivalent of all are these physical objects, which by rights ought to exhibit surface disorientation, pitting, or striae that might allow for some plausible interpretation.

Yet its true cost cannot be quantified in numbers. It is paid while dodging between a vagrancy charge and the newest electrical brain-curette; while subsisting on what the rich are bullied into giving, or what the poor willingly share while depriving themselves. 

It is more costly than ambergris, though its stench is not quite as loud. As a few wise men have noted, it is produced in the very same manner—vomited forth by sick whales. It is valuable for those exact qualities: its staying power and its depth of penetration. 

And for this, I have squandered every crying dime.
outputs.L2:
Here is a complete prose rewrite that retains all the original details while using fresh phrasing and sentence structures:

On May 17, 1955, in Seattle, Washington, a moment of acute realization occurs. Despite an intense, desperate longing for anything other than the current situation, there are no personal possessions, nor will there ever be anything beyond this immediate, unavoidable, and priceless moment—an experience so precious that no person can actually purchase it. 

Compact, almost rigid orange marigolds stand in view. Positioned behind them is a garage door painted pink with a foolish commercial shade called "Old Rose," a name that evokes memories of war. Without prompt or control, the mind wanders back past the physical enclosure, drawn to the striking combination of orange against pink and green. This mental drift cannot be justified or explained; it offers no rationale, leaving open the question of its worth or purpose in the face of impending death. 

With under a second left to live and attempt a rationale, one could argue that the visual phenomenon of orange set against pink is simply the result of light traveling at a specific velocity in defined wavelengths or oscillating energy clusters. Does this internal psychological impact of pure beauty hold greater value than a fine sirloin steak or an artistic screen crafted by Korin? 

Nothing serves as an equivalent—especially not the visible objects themselves, which fail to exhibit expected physical traits like surface warping, small depressions, or striated grooves that might allow for a logical explanation. Furthermore, the true price of this experience defies numerical calculation. It is incurred while navigating a life between arrests for vagrancy and modern psychiatric electro-treatments, surviving on food coerced from wealthy individuals or generously provided by the poor at personal sacrifice. 

This state is even costlier than ambergris, though its odor is less intense. As certain learned men have observed, ambergris is formed through the same process—expelled from the stomach of a sick whale—and commands immense worth due to the identical qualities of endurance and deep resonance. Ultimately, every single penny available has been completely wasted.
outputs.L3:
To the casual observer, my life might be defined entirely by scarcity. I possess no material wealth, no grand inheritance, and no physical property to call my own. Yet, beneath the weight of this poverty lies a secret, immediate wealth: an unyielding openness to the sensory present. Stripped of the distractions of ownership, I am forced into an acute intimacy with the world as it unfolds moment by moment, finding in the simple act of perception a priceless value that money could never purchase.

This truth struck me recently with overwhelming force during an ordinary walk. My eyes caught a sudden, violent collision of color: a cluster of vibrant orange marigolds blooming fiercely against the faded, peeling surface of a pink garage door. It was an improbable, unstudied aesthetic pairing, yet the visual contrast was so luminous that it arrested my steps entirely. In an instant, my mind was pulled into an uncontrollable, irrational wandering. Consciousness defied all logical order, tumbling down unbidden avenues of memory, emotion, and wonder that no rational thought could ever fully map or explain.

In moments like these, faced with the undeniable brevity of human life and our fleeting mortality, the limitations of objective intellect become glaringly obvious. A physicist might comfortably reduce that moment to mechanics, explaining the garage door and the petals as mere wavelengths of light absorbing and reflecting photons into the optic nerve. Yet, such scientific descriptions, precise as they may be, completely fail to capture the true, lived reality of the aesthetic experience. They explain *how* we see, but tell us nothing of *what it means* to be struck awake by color in a dying world. 

The profound internal impact of such beauty defies the language of commerce and intellect alike. The shift that occurs within the mind when confronted by raw aesthetic grace cannot be measured by numbers, cataloged by algorithms, or equaled by the quiet prestige of material possessions. Even the traditional, curated art hanging in pristine museums often feels pale beside these accidental, living masterpieces encountered on the street.

To live with a heart so defenselessly open to this raw aesthetic power carries a brutal price. It has cost me economic security, pushing me into a life marked by hardship, instability, and material lack. Yet, I find that these rare, transcendent encounters possess an enduring potency. Like ambergris—the mysterious, precious substance forged through internal distress and washed ashore to be prized above gold—the beauty harvested from a life of hardship retains an intoxicating, imperishable fragrance. It lingers long after the moment has passed, enriching the soul far beyond the reach of poverty.
outputs.L4:
There is an odd, stubborn violence to the way light hits a specific corner of the world, a sudden perceptual ambush that no amount of intellectual preparation can shield you from. I was walking down a narrow alleyway in Seattle—a city usually draped in an apologetic, diffuse grayness, where colors are softened as if viewed through wet tissue paper—when the visual noise of the everyday suddenly collapsed into a single, blinding point of focus. It was nothing grand. No mountain range, no cathedral, no vast Pacific horizon. Just a cluster of marigolds, hyper-saturated and screamingly orange, growing wild and untamed out of a crack in the concrete, set directly against the peeling paint of a dusty, salmon-pink garage door. 

My mind immediately began its desperate, habitual work of trying to tame it. Why *that* combination? Orange on pink—a pairing that by every rule of conventional design ought to clash, ought to feel garish, almost offensive. Yet there it was, humming with an electric, impossible resonance. I stood there on the wet asphalt, feeling the absurd impulse to measure it, to dismantle the moment like a clockmaker trying to find the tick in a spring. What was the exact nanometer of that reflected light? If I broke the scene down into its constituent parts—the chlorophyll in the stems, the lutein providing the petals' fiery pigment, the cheap acrylic resin flaking off the weathered wood of the door, the specific angle of a low afternoon sun breaking through cloud cover—would the math finally yield the reason for this sudden, breathless shock to my system?

We try so hard to translate these collisions into language or science. We want to speak of rods and cones, of optical nerves firing signals to the occipital lobe, of evolutionary biology tricking us into paying attention to bright colors because they once signaled ripe fruit or toxic danger. Or worse, we try to assign it a ledger value. What is the real estate worth? A decaying garage in a gentrifying neighborhood, worth hundreds of thousands of dollars on paper, while the blossoms themselves are essentially weeds, costing pennies in a paper seed packet. But standing there, the apparatus of rational reductionism feels utterly embarrassing, like trying to explain a symphony by weighing the violin.

The truth is that the visual hit of those marigolds against that pink paint did not care about its own components, nor did it ask for my permission to overwrite whatever trivial thoughts I had been carrying down the street. It possessed a terrifyingly direct authority. It penetrated the clutter of the day, burning itself into the back of my eyelids with an indelible staying power that felt almost physical, as if the color had been stamped directly onto the psyche. Hours later, long after leaving that alley, the image remained entirely undiminished by time or distance, glowing in the memory with the same strange, quiet fury.

This is the humbling terror of unmediated beauty. It resists every attempt at commodification; you cannot harvest that exact interplay of light, wood, and petal to put it in a vault or trade it on an exchange. It exists only in the brief, unrepeatable intersection of scene and observer. Yet, far from being a frivolous luxury—a temporary distraction from the "real" work of survival, commerce, and logic—this immediate, unquantifiable aesthetic jolt reveals itself as something far more urgent. It is an irreplaceable anchor. In a world relentlessly intent on flattening reality into data, metrics, and monetary transactions, the stubborn, irrational glow of orange against pink remains a priceless necessity, reminding the human mind that its deepest vitality lies in its capacity to simply be struck mute by the astonishing fact of the world.
outputs.L5:
The rain had a way of flattening the world, washing away the ambient noise until only a heavy, expectant silence remained. In that quiet space, Arthur stared at the blank sheet of paper resting beneath the warm glow of his desk lamp. He needed to write something—**anything**—that could mend the rift that had grown between them. 

For weeks, he had scoured his own memories, searching **desperately** for the exact moment everything had begun to fray. Was it a careless word spoken in haste? A slow, quiet negligence that had gradually solidified into a wall? He turned those past conversations over in his mind like jagged stones, searching for a single smooth edge he could use to build a foundation for forgiveness. He was ready to surrender his pride, to apologize without reservation, and to give whatever was asked of him just to hear her voice again.

He pressed the pen to the paper, the ink blooming into a small dark circle as he hesitated. The words were there, heavy and urgent, waiting to spill out. 

**But** as the tip of the pen began to move, a cold clarity settled over him. He realized the most painful truth of all: some silences are not invitations to fix what was broken. They are simply the quiet ending of a story that has already run its course.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness Beat poem set in 1950s Seattle that explores the intense, inescapable experience of color and beauty from the perspective of a destitute poet.
counterfactuals.output:
No nickels left in the frayed seams of my corduroys on Yesler Way, 
no bread in the belly, just the cold teeth of the Puget wind biting through a torn wool coat, 
but God—*the light!*—the light is a brass trumpet blasting through the grey steam of Skid Road!
I am drowning in a riot of chromes and cobalt, a ruined saint on a wooden dock, 
my eyes wide open and weeping visual mercury while the 5:00 p.m. streetcars spark electric-turquoise 
against the wet cables of 1955!

They think I’m mad, sitting on this rain-slicked curb with a stub of pencil and no shoes,
but they don’t see the neon Rainier Beer sign bleeding molten rubies into the asphalt oil-slick,
a glowing violet puddle that reflects the entire holy catastrophe of the sky!
It’s too much—it’s an assault!—the blue is screaming from the belly of the bay,
ultramarine, navy, indigo-shuddering water slapping against the creosote pilings,
and the fishmongers at Pike Place tossing silver salmon through air that smells like crushed marigolds and wet copper!

Look at the orange! The terrifying, unasked-for, agonizing orange of a crate of persimmons,
a sunburst of pure cadmium exploding against the wet cedar boards!
I try to close my eyelids but the color bleeds right through the skin—
a yellow sun burning behind the smog, lemon-raw, butter-gold, a blinding saxophone howl of yellow 
that shakes the glass of the pawnshop windows where dusty saxes dream of Kansas City.
I am penniless! I am starving! But I am bathed in the imperial purple of the overcast twilight,
a bruised, velvet sky hanging low over the spine of the Olympic range,
snow-peaks glowing like pink teeth in the last desperate gasps of the Pacific sun!

How can a man ask for a dime for soup when he is being crucified by emerald?
The moss on the brick alleyways—holy moss!—glaring like electric radium in the damp,
the green of pine needles, the green of deep-sea kelp, the green of a million Douglas firs 
surrounding this damp timber-town like a choir of green giants screaming *LIVE! LIVE! LIVE!*
I walk past the steam-hissing diners, eyes burning, optic nerves fried by the beauty of a bruised apple,
the scarlet sheen of a red-headed girl’s scarf flashing down Second Avenue like a stray flame in the fog,
the silver mist wrapping Smith Tower in a veil of spun pewter, translucent, shimmering, absolute!

I have no roof! I have no dime! I have only this terrifying, inescapable optic ecstasy!
The rain isn't wet, it's a thousand liquid diamonds falling through the yellow haze of the streetlamps!
Seattle is a prism! Seattle is a shattered stained-glass window melted by jazz and rain!
I collapse on a bench by the ferry terminal, drunk on no wine but the blinding, hallucinatory turquoise of the tide,
beaten senseless by the majesty of the world, 
a destitute king crowned in neon, 
choking on the golden, glorious, unforgiving beauty of it all!
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a poem timestamped "(Seattle, Washington 17 May, 1955)" that incorporates the following elements: orange marigolds, a garage door painted "Old Rose", scientific wave-lengths of light, poverty/electroshock therapy, and a comparison of beauty's value to ambergris.
counterfactuals.output:
**(Seattle, Washington 17 May, 1955)**

The Puget mist divides the afternoon 
into strict, invisible frequencies—
six hundred nanometers of scattered orange
caught in the alley’s damp and heavy air.
Against the gravel, the garage door painted *Old Rose*
flakes off in pale, dusty ribbons,
while at its base, a line of marigolds 
ignites the dirt with bitter, copper flare.

We have no dime left for the gas, no bread
to soften on the chipped tin plate. 
You sit on the bottom step, your fingers twitching
with the residual current of the state hospital’s cure.
They strapped your arms; they greased your temples raw,
then sent one hundred volts of lightning through your skull
to burn out the depression of the poor,
as if a violent spark could strike an empty cupboard into light.

Your memory is a smoldering, blank field.
You ask me what the flowers are, and why they smell like rust.

I sit beside you in the wet May chill
and tell you beauty has no gentle origin.
It is like ambergris—
that dark, morbid secretion from a whale’s bruised gut,
vomited into the salt tides, heavy and foul,
yet bought by kings for its weight in gold
because it binds the fleeting scent of roses to the skin.

This poverty, this violent voltage in your brain,
is the deep sea’s agony brought to shore.
And these vivid, jagged flowers by the *Old Rose* door
are what we salvage from the wreck:
a precious, stubborn perfume
fixed against the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem about the overwhelming sensory impact of everyday visual beauty when you have no money left to your name.
counterfactuals.output:
The bank account is silence, cold and clean,
No copper left to rattle in the coat.
Yet out the window, sunset, bruised and green,
Pours like a heavy amber down the throat.

When you have nothing left to buy or keep,
The world demands you take it through the eyes.
The senses wake while all your prospects sleep,
And hyper-vivid colors start to rise.

The rain-slicked asphalt turns to melted glass,
Catching the neon of a neon sign—
A cheap motel becomes a stained-glass mass,
A glowing cathedral of oil and brine.

The produce stand is agonizing, bright:
The lacquered crimson of the radish skin,
The wet, saffron lemons in the light—
A rich museum I am standing in.

A plastic bag caught high upon a wire
Fills with the gale and gathers up the noon,
Igniting like a ball of holy fire,
A fragile, blinding, floating yellow moon.

There is a cruelty in a world so fine
To one who cannot pay for bed or bread.
The light is free, an incandescent wine,
Poured lavishly on one who isn't fed.

I am so poor my vision has grown raw,
Stripped of the noise of transaction and choice.
I stand paralyzed, held in terrified awe
By a universe shouting in shimmering voice.

I walk through riches that I cannot spend,
A pauper drowning in a prism sea,
Where daylight squanders, reckless to the end,
Its endless, crushing glimmers upon me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a modernist, fragmented poem in the style of mid-century American poetry exploring color contrast (orange against pink), perception theory, and the true cost of aesthetic experience?
counterfactuals.output:
**STUDY IN CADMIUM AND MADDER (THE OPTIC LEDGER)**


**I.**

The eye is a machine of refusal.

	Orange—
	(zinc-struck, heavy as a marigold in oil)
		plunged into
	Pink.

Not harmony. A violence at the margin.
Look long enough:
the boundary line shimmers,
	a gray ghost generated by the fovea,
	a refusal of the brain to synthesize.

The retina demands a truce
it will not be granted.


**II.**

Albers wrote: *Color deceives continuously.*

		A cone cell fires—
	590 nanometers (citrus, hazard, flame)
		tangled with
	630 (flesh, carnation, pink of the abattoir).

The mind pays for this geometry
with the coin of the present.
	To see the orange vibrate against the rose
	is to un-see
		the dust on the frame,
		the clock in the hall,
		the war on the back page.

Perception is an act of erasure.


**III.**

What is the tariff on pure sight?

		[   Field note:
		    The miner coughs in the cadmium pit
		    so the canvas may hold this glare.   ]

The pink does not soften the orange.
It accuses it.

A luxury of the nervous system:
to sit in the climate-controlled gallery,
abstracting the blood
into a question of hue.

		We call it *taste.*
		The ledger calls it *debt.*


**IV.**

		Fragment:
		*vision is not receipt;*
		*it is extraction.*

The nerve tires.
After three minutes, the orange turns to liver;
the pink subsides into salt.

	We buy the thrill of the friction
	by starving the center.

You step back into the street.
The light is gray, un-curated, free—
and for a moment,
you cannot afford it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem about an impoverished man staring at marigolds in front of a pink wall, connecting the raw physical phenomenon of sight to themes of madness, squandered money, and whale vomit.
counterfactuals.output:
Through the torn curtain of a clouded lens,
Four hundred nanometers of violent bloom
Strike the wet glass. The ray of summer bends,
A physics of starvation in the gloom.
Against a wall of peeling, chalky pink—
The shade of fevered skin or boiled meat—
The marigolds ignite. His pupils shrink,
Refracting gold he can no longer eat.

It is a mechanical, chemical thing:
Photons crashing into rod and cone,
A micro-burst of electricity, a sting
That travels up the optic tract alone.
Yet in that instant, as the image flips
Right-side-up inside his hollow brain,
The raw impulse of seeing slowly slips
Into the architecture of his pain.

The orange petals flare like spent doubloons,
The brassy sovereigns wasted in his youth,
Poured down the throats of taverns and saloons,
Squandered in pursuit of fleeting truth.
His eye takes in the light and counts the cost:
Each wave of yellow light, a vanished note,
A phantom fortune he long since had lost,
Now mockingly dangled before his throat.

And visual processing, overloaded, churns—
The light turns waxy, thick, corrupt, and deep.
The mind, by long insomnia corroded,
Drifts where the leviathans of sickness sleep.
For what is sight but Ambergris?—the spew
Of deep-sea whales, a dark and greasy bile
Cast up from depths of ocean-black and blue,
Fermenting on the beach in rank defile?

Yes—sight is whale-vomit! A stomach turned,
A foul secretion of the brain's dark gut,
Where rotten, oceanic grief is churned
To make a perfume for the eyelid’s shut.
He stares until the precious ambergris
Of visual light turns pungent, rich, and mad;
The squandered gold, the ocean’s sick release,
Are all the currency he ever had.

Unblinking now before the plaster blush,
His optic nerve ablaze with sacred rust,
He stands enthralled within the sensory rush,
A king of rags, digesting golden dust.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
